It's been... months. Actually, about a year and two months ago. That's when things really started unraveling. I had to move into that smaller rental right after my divorce.

Voices? Well... I mean, I hear the radio. My scanner. Even when it's completely turned off and just sitting on the kitchen counter, I hear it. I... I don't know. Like I said, I haven't really felt normal in a long time. So I can't really say if there was a week or two where I felt fine but still heard the scanner. It's just always there. \n\nYou know, the scanner used to sit right next to this old coffee maker I had. A standard drip machine, nothing fancy. But it had this warming plate that would scorch the bottom of the pot if you left it on too long. It made the whole kitchen smell like burnt toast and old pennies. I tried to clean the burnt stains off the glass with baking soda and vinegar once. My mother swore by baking soda for everything. She used to keep an open box in the back of the refrigerator to absorb odors. Always the yellow box. I think they still make it the exact same way. But she'd forget to change it, so the box would just sit there for years, getting hard as a rock. You could probably use it as a doorstop. \n\nWe had a heavy iron doorstop at the precinct, shaped like a bulldog. Some rookie tripped over it once and nearly broke his ankle. He had to wear this clunky walking boot for six weeks, and it squeaked every time he took a step on the linoleum. Squeak, squeak, squeak. Drove everyone insane. He ended up transferring out to a different district... \n\nAnyway, I don't really know about the weeks or the mood. I just... I don't have a good answer for that.\n\nDoctor: Going back further than the past year—say, two or three years ago, before your divorce—did you ever hear those scanner-like voices or see the shadow, even when you were feeling completely fine?\n\nPatient: Before the divorce? Everything just kind of blends together. \n\nI do remember the day she left, though. She packed all her things into these cardboard boxes we got from the liquor store down the street. It had this little red float inside, kind of like the bobber you use for fishing. I haven't been fishing since I was a kid. My dad used to take me out to Miller's Pond, and we'd sit on these aluminum folding chairs that would get blisteringly hot in the sun. If you wore shorts, the backs of your thighs would just roast...\n\nBut, sorry, what were you asking? Before the divorce? Yeah, I don't know. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Right now? Well, no, not right this exact second. It's usually when I'm at home. I'll have the scanner turned completely off, you know, because sometimes you just need quiet after a shift. But even with it off, I hear these... short bursts. Like radio chatter. It's usually warning me, telling me someone is inside the house or that I'm being watched. And then there's the shadow. I'll see it move past the hallway, just out of the corner of my eye. I'll clear every room, check all the closets, behind the doors—standard procedure. You always check behind the doors because that's a blind spot. 

We learned that at the academy. They set up these mock rooms with cardboard cutouts of bad guys. If you didn't check the corner behind the door, the instructor would blow an air horn right in your ear. My ears rang for three days after my first room-clearing drill. The instructor, Sergeant Miller, he had this thick mustache that completely covered his upper lip. Reminded me of a walrus. He used to chew on these wooden matchsticks all day long. He'd just roll them from one side of his mouth to the other. I tried doing that once with a toothpick, but I accidentally bit down on it and got a splinter stuck right in my gums. Took me half an hour in front of the bathroom mirror with tweezers to get it out. Tweezers are so hard to grip when your hands are wet. I had just washed my hands with that cheap pink soap they have in public restrooms. It always smells like artificial cherries...

But, no, I'm not hearing them right now in your office. It's mostly at home, like I said. The warnings and the shadow in the hall.

The instructor, Sergeant Miller, he had this thick mustache that completely covered his upper lip. Reminded me of a walrus. He used to chew on these wooden matchsticks all day long. He'd just roll them from one side of his mouth to the other. I tried doing that once with a toothpick, but I accidentally bit down on it and got a splinter stuck right in my gums. Took me half an hour in front of the bathroom mirror with tweezers to get it out. Tweezers are so hard to grip when your hands are wet. A whole month without them? No, no, it's been pretty constant lately. The voices, those shadows, and that feeling—that absolute certainty that people are tracking me—it's been going on for about four months now. Every single day for four months. 

Four months ago was October, right around Halloween. I always hated Halloween when I was on patrol. Kids running out into the street in dark costumes, teenagers smashing pumpkins... I remember one year, this kid threw a pumpkin off an overpass and it hit a patrol car. Smashed the windshield right in. The glass safety film held it together, though. That film is incredible stuff. I still have my dad's dog tags in a cigar box somewhere. The box smells like cedar and old tobacco. It's a nice smell. Not like the smell of burning leaves, which always makes my throat itch. My neighbor burns his leaves every fall, even though there's a city ordinance against it. I should probably report him, but... 

What was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, four months. It hasn't stopped for a whole month at all. Just four months of it, straight through.

Between the divorce and... four months ago? I don't know, it's hard to say. I guess it was just the same. Just that heavy feeling, not wanting to do anything. I don't remember feeling like my old self at all.

Well... I mean, I hear the radio. My scanner. Even when it's completely turned off and just sitting on the kitchen counter, I hear it. It's one of those older, heavy-duty models with the thick rubber antenna. My old partner, Dave, he used to chew on the end of his antenna during night shifts. Completely ruined the casing. Dave had this weird habit of eating sunflower seeds and spitting the shells into a paper cup, but he'd always miss, and they'd end up in the cruiser's cup holder. It drove me crazy because they'd get all sticky with spilled coffee. He drank his coffee black, but he always bought it from this gas station that burned the beans. \n\nAnyway, the scanner... it's off, but I still hear these short, static-y bursts coming from it. Like dispatch, but it's not dispatch. It's these voices, and they're usually warning me. They tell me that someone is inside the house, or that I'm being watched right that second. \n\nAnd I know how to clear a building, right? I do it by the book. I take my flashlight—the heavy Maglite that takes four D batteries. You can't even buy D batteries at the corner store anymore, you have to go all the way to the big box store on Route 9, and the one near me always smells like fertilizer because the garden center is right by the entrance. They had a massive sale on mulch last week, bags piled up to the ceiling. But I use the flashlight and I clear every single room in that rental. Every closet, under the bed, checking the corners. But even after I've cleared every room and I know nobody is there... I'll still see this shadow. Just sliding past the hallway wall, right out of the corner of my eye.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed whether these voices and shadow-like visions only happen when you're feeling really down and low, or do they also occur during times when your mood feels okay?\n\nPatient: When I feel okay? I... I don't really know. I haven't kept track of that. I guess I haven't really felt \"okay\" in a long time anyway, so it's hard to compare. \n\nI used to feel okay when I'd take my patrol cruiser through the automatic car wash at the end of my shift, though. The one on 5th Street. The guys at the precinct always gave me grief because I'd pay out of pocket for the premium wash with that tri-color foam. It sprayed pink, blue, and yellow all over the windshield, and it smelled exactly like artificial cherry. Like those hard cough drops my grandmother used to keep wrapped in tissues in her purse. She had this heavy leather purse with a brass snap-clasp that sounded almost like a small caliber gunshot when she closed it. Real thick, heavy leather. You just don't see craftsmanship like that anymore, everything is synthetic now. I bought a synthetic winter coat last November and the zipper teeth misaligned on the very second day I wore it. You try to fix it, but once the plastic bends, it's just ruined. \n\nBut... wait, what were you asking? About the shadows? I don't really know when they happen.\n\nDoctor: Did you start hearing these scanner voices and seeing the shadow before you began feeling depressed, or did they start around the same time as the low mood?\n\nPatient: Before or same time? I... I'm not really sure which came first. It all just sort of bleeds together now. I used to keep track of everything, every little detail, in this tiny spiral notebook. A pocket one, you know? Fits right in the breast pocket of the uniform. \n\nThe spiral wire on those things always used to catch on the fabric, though, and it would pull these little blue threads out. My ex-wife hated when I brought those shirts home to wash because the threads would tangle up in the machine. We had this old top-loading washer that sounded exactly like a helicopter taking off during the spin cycle. The repair guy said the drum was unbalanced, but he charged eighty bucks just to walk through the door and look at it. Eighty bucks! And he tracked mud all over the kitchen linoleum. It was that sticky, red clay kind of mud. You only really see that specific kind of clay out past the county line near the old brickyard. \n\nWe had a call out there once, some kids trespassing, and my boots were covered in that red clay for a week. The tread on those tactical boots is so deep, it's basically impossible to clean out. You have to use a toothpick or a flathead screwdriver to dig the dried mud out of the grooves. I lost my favorite flathead screwdriver doing that. It had a yellow handle... \n\nBut, I'm sorry, the timeline. Yeah, I couldn't tell you. I really don't know if the low mood started before the scanner voices or not. It's just all happening.\n\nDoctor: Thinking back over the past year, has there ever been a stretch of time—even just a week or two—when your mood felt normal or better, but you were still hearing the scanner voices or seeing that shadow?\n\nPatient: Normal or better? I... I don't know. Like I said, I haven't really felt normal in a long time. So I can't really say if there was a week or two where I felt fine but still heard the scanner. It's just always there. \n\nYou know, the scanner used to sit right next to this old coffee maker I had. A standard drip machine, nothing fancy. But it had this warming plate that would scorch the bottom of the pot if you left it on too long. It made the whole kitchen smell like burnt toast and old pennies. I tried to clean the burnt stains off the glass with baking soda and vinegar once. My mother swore by baking soda for everything. She used to keep an open box in the back of the refrigerator to absorb odors. Always the yellow box. I think they still make it the exact same way. But she'd forget to change it, so the box would just sit there for years, getting hard as a rock. You could probably use it as a doorstop. \n\nWe had a heavy iron doorstop at the precinct, shaped like a bulldog. Some rookie tripped over it once and nearly broke his ankle. He had to wear this clunky walking boot for six weeks, and it squeaked every time he took a step on the linoleum. Squeak, squeak, squeak. Drove everyone insane. He ended up transferring out to a different district... \n\nAnyway, I don't really know about the weeks or the mood. I just... I don't have a good answer for that.\n\nDoctor: Going back further than the past year—say, two or three years ago, before your divorce—did you ever hear those scanner-like voices or see the shadow, even when you were feeling completely fine?\n\nPatient: Before the divorce? Two or three years ago? I... I really couldn't tell you. It's so hard to remember what \"fine\" even felt like back then. Everything just kind of blends together. \n\nI do remember the day she left, though. She packed all her things into these cardboard boxes we got from the liquor store down the street. The ones with the dividers inside for the wine bottles. You have to pull those cardboard dividers out if you want to fit anything bigger than a pair of shoes in them. I used one of those dividers to organize my socket wrenches in the garage, actually. It worked pretty well until the humidity got to it and the cardboard got all soft and warped. \n\nGarages always get so damp in the summer. We had this dehumidifier out there, but you had to remember to empty the little plastic bucket every two days or it would shut off automatically. It had this little red float inside, kind of like the bobber you use for fishing. I haven't been fishing since I was a kid. My dad used to take me out to Miller's Pond, and we'd sit on these aluminum folding chairs that would get blisteringly hot in the sun. If you wore shorts, the backs of your thighs would just roast...\n\nBut, sorry, what were you asking? Before the divorce? Yeah, I don't know. I can't remember if I heard the voices or saw the shadow back then when I was feeling okay. I just don't know.\n\nDoctor: Right now, as we're sitting here talking, are you hearing the scanner voices or seeing the shadow at this very moment?\n\nPatient: Right now? Well, no, not right this exact second. It's usually when I'm at home. I'll have the scanner turned completely off, you know, because sometimes you just need quiet after a shift. But even with it off, I hear these... short bursts. Like radio chatter. It's usually warning me, telling me someone is inside the house or that I'm being watched. And then there's the shadow. I'll see it move past the hallway, just out of the corner of my eye. I'll clear every room, check all the closets, behind the doors—standard procedure. You always check behind the doors because that's a blind spot. \n\nWe learned that at the academy. They set up these mock rooms with cardboard cutouts of bad guys. If you didn't check the corner behind the door, the instructor would blow an air horn right in your ear. My ears rang for three days after my first room-clearing drill. The instructor, Sergeant Miller, he had this thick mustache that completely covered his upper lip. Reminded me of a walrus. He used to chew on these wooden matchsticks all day long. He'd just roll them from one side of his mouth to the other. I tried doing that once with a toothpick, but I accidentally bit down on it and got a splinter stuck right in my gums. Took me half an hour in front of the bathroom mirror with tweezers to get it out. Tweezers are so hard to grip when your hands are wet. I had just washed my hands with that cheap pink soap they have in public restrooms. It always smells like artificial cherries...\n\nBut, no, I'm not hearing them right now in your office. It's mostly at home, like I said. The warnings and the shadow in the hall.\n\nDoctor: Aside from low motivation, can you tell me how your sleep and appetite have been over the past couple of months—are you sleeping and eating more or less than usual?\n\nPatient: Sleep and appetite? I don't know, I haven't really been paying attention to either of those things. I guess they're just... normal? I don't really know what normal is anymore, but I haven't noticed any big changes. \n\nI usually just eat whatever is easy. Canned soup, mostly. Chicken noodle. But you have to be careful with the pull-tab cans. I sliced my thumb open on one of those lids a few years back. The cut was so clean I didn't even feel it at first, just saw the blood dripping onto the linoleum. It was a pain to clean up. I had to use bleach, and the smell of bleach always reminds me of the community pool I went to as a kid. \n\nThey used so much chlorine in that pool, your eyes would burn for hours after you got out. My mom used to make me wear these tight, neon green swim trunks. They had a little mesh lining inside that was incredibly uncomfortable. I always tried to cut it out with scissors, but I'd just end up fraying the edges. We had these heavy, dull scissors with orange plastic handles. They couldn't cut through anything thicker than a piece of paper. My dad used them to trim his mustache, which never made any sense to me. He had a really thick mustache, kind of like Sergeant Miller, actually. But my dad's was always a little lopsided. \n\nAnyway, I don't think my sleep or eating has changed much. Just the usual, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Has there ever been a stretch of at least a month, at any point, when you did not hear the scanner voices or see the shadow at all?\n\nPatient: A whole month without them? No, no, it's been pretty constant lately. The voices, those shadows, and that feeling—that absolute certainty that people are tracking me—it's been going on for about four months now. Every single day for four months. \n\nFour months ago was October, right around Halloween. I always hated Halloween when I was on patrol. Kids running out into the street in dark costumes, teenagers smashing pumpkins... I remember one year, this kid threw a pumpkin off an overpass and it hit a patrol car. Smashed the windshield right in. The glass safety film held it together, though. That film is incredible stuff. They use something similar on the windows of banks, you know, to stop bullets. Or at least slow them down. I had to go to the bank last week to get a cashier's check, and they had these new pens chained to the desks. The chains were made of those little metal beads, like the ones on dog tags. I still have my dad's dog tags in a cigar box somewhere. The box smells like cedar and old tobacco. It's a nice smell. Not like the smell of burning leaves, which always makes my throat itch. My neighbor burns his leaves every fall, even though there's a city ordinance against it. I should probably report him, but... \n\nWhat was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, four months. It hasn't stopped for a whole month at all. Just four months of it, straight through.\n\nDoctor: Thinking about the time between your divorce and about four months ago—before the scanner voices and shadow started—did the low mood and loss of interest stay the same the whole time, or was there any stretch where you felt more like your old self during those months?\n\nPatient: Between the divorce and... four months ago? I don't know, it's hard to say. I guess it was just the same. Just that heavy feeling, not wanting to do anything. I don't remember feeling like my old self at all. \n\nMy old self used to love fishing. I had this great little aluminum boat, a 14-footer. Perfect for getting into the shallows where the bass like to hide. The guy I bought it from had painted it this awful camouflage pattern, but he used interior house paint, so it started flaking off the first time I took it out. Little green and brown chips floating in the water. It looked like fish food, actually. I tried feeding fish in a pond once with breadcrumbs, but I read later that bread is terrible for them. It swells up in their stomachs. You're supposed to give them peas instead. Frozen peas, thawed out. My ex-wife used to put frozen peas on her eyes when she had a headache. She said the cold helped with the swelling, but I always thought she just looked ridiculous lying on the couch with vegetables on her face. She bought the generic brand peas, too. The bag always had more ice crystals than actual peas. Ice crystals remind me of the frost that builds up on the inside of my freezer. I need to defrost it, but it's such a hassle. You have to take everything out, put it in coolers... \n\nBut yeah, no. I don't think there was any stretch where I felt better. Just the same low mood the whole time.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out.
